hints.title: Translate direction into derivative signs
hints.body: Differentiate both functions: f′(x)=6(x+2) and g′(x)=3(x+1)(x+3). We need opposite directions.
hints.recap: Function increase or decrease is determined by its derivative sign, not by its y-value.
hints.pitfall: A function can be negative and increasing.
hints.pause: Mark the derivative zeros <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> in order.

recall.reminder: Function increase or decrease is determined by its derivative sign, not by its y-value.

hints.title: Intersect the opposite-sign regions
hints.body: f′ is negative before −2 and positive after. The upward quadratic g′ is positive outside [−3,−1] and negative inside.
hints.recap: Use one shared sign chart to compare two derivatives.
hints.pitfall: The requested condition includes either function being the increasing one.
hints.pause: Find both regions where the derivative signs differ.

recall.reminder: Use one shared sign chart to compare two derivatives.

hints.title: Match the endpoint convention
hints.body: Use your sign chart to select every interval where the derivative signs oppose. The offered answers include stationary boundary points using nonnegative and nonpositive derivative conditions.
hints.recap: Check how boundary points are included when expressing the intervals.
hints.pitfall: A stationary derivative is zero; do not describe it as strictly positive or strictly negative.
hints.pause: State the complete union, including the stationary boundaries required by this convention.

recall.reminder: Check how boundary points are included when expressing the intervals.

solution:
f′(x)=6(x+2) and g′(x)=3(x+1)(x+3). For x<−3, the first is negative and the second positive. For −2<x<−1, the first is positive and the second negative. On the remaining open intervals they have the same sign.

Using the non-strict endpoint convention of the answer options, include the stationary boundaries. The result is x≤−3 or −2≤x≤−1.

Answer E. The endpoints have a zero derivative, rather than two strictly opposite derivative signs.
